clue.text: A sweet sorrow denied to the bald.

blocks.note: first meaning: Juliet's farewell, 'such sweet sorrow' in Romeo and Juliet
second meaning: the line where the hair is combed two ways, which a bald head cannot have

explanation.surface: A wistful line about a sadness that bald men are spared.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's 'Parting is such sweet sorrow' gives the first half; the second is the line combed into a head of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a farewell between people and the dividing line in combed hair.

clue.text: After what has actually happened, the alternative is to produce the minister.

indicators.note: 'After' says the second piece is placed following the first one in the answer

blocks.note: events that have really happened are in the past
OR is the word that offers an alternative

explanation.surface: A puzzled remark about making a minister appear once events have taken place.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastor is a Christian clergyman in charge of a congregation, so a minister of religion.

clue.text: Some people can't stand it.

blocks.note: surface reading: some people are unable to stay on their feet
setter's reading: some people cannot put up with a loud din

explanation.surface: A sweeping remark that some people cannot bear a certain thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't stand' means can't bear; the thing many people cannot bear is a loud noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a loud, unpleasant noise, the sort of din plenty of people find intolerable.

clue.text: The law interferes with their business, though without some of them there might be little law.

definitions.text: The law interferes with their business, though without some of them there might be little law

blocks.clueFragment: The law interferes with their business
blocks.note: first reading: licensing laws restrict the trade of public houses and their opening hours

blocks.clueFragment: without some of them there might be little law
blocks.note: second reading: the London societies that train and call every English barrister, without which there would be few lawyers

explanation.surface: A grumble that the law meddles in some trade that the law itself depends on.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word covers pubs, hemmed in by licensing law, and the Inns of Court, the London societies to which every English barrister belongs.
explanation.definitionFit: Inns are public houses whose trade the licensing laws regulate, and the Inns of Court produce the barristers.

clue.text: Suggests it may sometimes be good thing to waive the profit.

definitions.text: Suggests it may sometimes be good thing to waive the profit

blocks.note: surface reading: a trader giving up a margin seems a poor idea
setter's reading: a purchase so cheap that the seller made nothing on it is a 'good' one for the buyer

explanation.surface: A merchant's maxim that going without a profit can sometimes pay off.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes something that is good precisely because the seller made no profit on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain is something bought cheaply, a good deal for the buyer because the seller has given up their margin.

clue.text: With the middle of the whole the fruit appears.

definitions.text: With the middle of the whole the fruit appears

blocks.note: surface reading: some central part of a larger thing
setter's reading: the flowering from which a tree's fruit grows

explanation.surface: A riddle about fruit showing up at the centre of something whole.
explanation.walkthrough: The fruit forms where the flowers were, which fits the answer; the phrase 'the middle of the whole' is not fully accounted for here, so treat this parse as partial.
explanation.definitionFit: Blossom is the flowering of a fruit tree, and the fruit develops from it.

clue.text: This may be crescent.

blocks.note: surface reading: a curved shape, like the new moon or a curved street
setter's reading: a piece of bread baked in a curved shape, as the French croissant (crescent) is

explanation.surface: A hint that something may take the shape of a crescent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crescent' points to the moon or a street, but the setter means a bread roll; croissant is French for crescent.
explanation.definitionFit: A croissant is a crescent-shaped bread roll, so a roll may indeed be crescent.

clue.text: Obviously full of spirit, and hasn't she a heavenly name?

blocks.note: the name visibly holds a heavenly spirit within its spelling
a girl's name taken from the word for a messenger of heaven

explanation.surface: Praise for a lively girl whose name sounds celestial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full of spirit' looks like lively, but it means the name contains an angel, a heavenly spirit, plus one more letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Angela is a woman's name derived from angel, the heavenly messenger, so it is literally a heavenly name.

clue.text: Untidy (anag.).

clue.text: Some are necessary in a ring but ten has a fatal sound.

definitions.text: Some are necessary in a ring

blocks.clueFragment: Some are necessary in a ring
blocks.note: first meaning: a boxer's attendants in the corner of the ring

explanation.surface: A boxing note: helpers are needed in the ring, but the count of ten spells defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves stay in the boxing ring: the corner men, and the ten-count that ends a bout.
explanation.definitionFit: Seconds are a boxer's corner assistants, and also the time units of the referee's fatal count of ten.

clue.text: In such wise we may be compelled to be grateful.

linkWords: In such wise we may be

explanation.surface: A wry observation that gratitude is sometimes forced on us.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence, but its two adjectives are separate senses of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Obliged means required by duty or force, and in polite usage also indebted or thankful.

clue.text: Should the lover lose his head, it may well be this as far as he is concerned.

definitions.text: it may well be this as far as he is concerned
definitions.note: 'this' stands for the answer: the affair is finished for him

indicators.note: losing a head means the opening letter of the word is cut away

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: If a suitor loses his head over someone, the romance may be finished for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose his head' sounds like falling madly in love; it means drop the L.
explanation.definitionFit: If the affair is over as far as he is concerned, it has ended for him.

clue.text: This will bring you up to scratch.

definitions.text: This will bring you up to scratch

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom for meeting the required standard

blocks.clueFragment: This will bring you up to scratch
blocks.note: setter's reading: something given by scratching the skin, as smallpox inoculation was

explanation.surface: A promise of something that will get you up to the required standard.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1930 smallpox protection was given by scratching it into the arm, so it literally brought you to a scratch.
explanation.definitionFit: A vaccine is a preparation giving immunity, once administered through a scratch on the skin.

clue.text: Rejected as it ought to be, seeing the danger so appropriately concealed in the red

indicators.note: something concealed in another thing sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

linkWords: as it ought to be, seeing

blocks.note: taken as written
the burning cord that sets off an explosive, the dangerous part

explanation.surface: A dangerous thing hidden in red, the colour of danger, is fittingly turned away.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's joke is that red is the danger colour, so it is apt to hide a danger in it.
explanation.definitionFit: To be refused is to be turned down or declined, the same as being rejected.

clue.text: Decidedly out of place here.

blocks.note: surface reading: something that does not belong in its setting
setter's reading: in the pages of a respectable newspaper, where bad language would never be printed

explanation.surface: A firm note that something does not belong in this setting.
explanation.walkthrough: This answer rests on the crossing letters and the reading that swearing has no place in The Times; treat it as unconfirmed until the published key arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath or swear word would be thoroughly improper in a dignified newspaper.

clue.text: Penny wise, pound foolish.

blocks.note: surface reading: the proverb about saving pennies while wasting pounds
setter's reading: a coin opening on a vending machine takes a penny, but a pound would never fit it

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is taken literally: penny-in-the-slot machines took pennies, and a pound (then a note or sovereign) would be foolish in one.
explanation.definitionFit: A slot is the narrow opening in a coin-operated machine, sized for a penny.

clue.text: Arranged, and if it's to be up or down,.the latter is-much more pleasant.

blocks.note: first reading: fixed or agreed, as a matter is

blocks.clueFragment: if it's to be up or down,.the latter is-much more pleasant
blocks.note: second reading: settling up means paying a bill, while settling down means making yourself comfortable

explanation.surface: A matter is fixed, and of the two directions, going down is nicer.
explanation.walkthrough: The word pairs with 'up' (pay what you owe) or 'down' (get comfortable), and the clue prefers the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Settled means decided or fixed, as an arranged matter is; and the phrasal verbs give paying up or relaxing.

clue.text: Don't miss it.

blocks.note: surface reading: an urging not to overlook some event
setter's reading: a public road vehicle that you can fail to catch at the stop

explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't miss it' sounds like an advertisement; the setter means a vehicle you might fail to catch, as in 'missing the bus'.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus is the full old name for a bus, the public vehicle people hurry not to miss.

clue.text: Scolds.

blocks.note: surface reading: a noun, nagging people
setter's reading: a verb, tells off angrily, an old sense of the answer word

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the old verb meaning to berate, not the usual sense of charges or prices.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone, in older English, is to reprove them angrily, the same as to scold.

clue.text: We can understand this mythological gentleman acting the goat.

definitions.text: this mythological gentleman acting the goat

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom for fooling about
setter's reading: a woodland creature of Greek myth, half man and half goat

explanation.surface: We can sympathise with a legendary figure who plays the fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acting the goat' means fooling around, but this figure literally is part goat.
explanation.definitionFit: A satyr is a lustful woodland god of Greek myth, with a man's body and goat's legs.

clue.text: This side of life is a sad theme.

blocks.note: surface reading: some aspect of existence
setter's reading: the sordid side of life, a gloomy subject for a writer

explanation.surface: A melancholy remark that one aspect of existence makes a sad subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'the seamy side of life' means its sordid, unpleasant aspect, a gloomy theme.

clue.text: Everything in this is a substitute.

definitions.text: Everything in this is a substitute

explanation.surface: A complaint that everything somewhere is a replacement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In his ___' means in his place; whatever stands 'in' this word is a stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: Stead means place or role, as in 'instead' and 'in his stead', so whatever is in it replaces another.

clue.text: This is an asset in a dog's life.

explanation.walkthrough: This answer is a guess fitting the crossing letters, not a confirmed parse; it will be checked against the published key.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare is food provided, which for a dog is the high point of its daily existence.

clue.text: Gives handy cover for a prize-fight.

definitions.text: Gives handy cover for a prize-fight

explanation.surface: Something provides a convenient excuse for staging a boxing match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handy' means convenient on the surface, but literally it is cover for the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitt is a glove or mitten, slang for a boxing glove and for the fist itself.

clue.text: Not meant for ridicule, as your boy may be one himself.

definitions.note: an old verb sense, given here only to be set aside

blocks.note: first meaning: an old verb, to reject with scorn, which the clue says is not the sense wanted

blocks.clueFragment: your boy may be one himself

explanation.surface: A warning not to mock something, since your own son might belong to it.
explanation.walkthrough: To scout an idea once meant to dismiss it scornfully; the clue rules that sense out in favour of the youth movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy who has joined the Scouts, the youth movement founded by Baden-Powell, is one himself.

clue.text: A moral substitute.

blocks.note: surface reading: the lesson of a story
setter's reading, tentatively: another word standing in for a moral principle

explanation.surface: Something offered as a stand-in on grounds of conscience.
explanation.walkthrough: This answer fits the crossing letters but is not fully parsed, so it is unconfirmed until the published key.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a moral principle, so it can stand in for the word 'moral' used as a noun.

clue.text: A man of no position expects to hold the reins in India

explanation.surface: A political jibe about a nobody hoping to take charge of India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold the reins' suggests governing; here it is literal, the job of an Indian groom.
explanation.definitionFit: A syce is a groom or stable servant in India, a lowly post that involves holding horses.

clue.text: Rarely raised singly.

blocks.note: surface reading: something like a child brought up alone
setter's reading: a feature of the face usually lifted together with its partner in surprise

explanation.surface: Something is seldom brought up on its own.

clue.text: This bird has caused rather a mix-up of late.

explanation.definitionFit: The teal is a small freshwater duck, so a bird.

clue.text: The devil's own profession!

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom for something very hard, as in 'the devil's own job'

explanation.walkthrough: 'The devil's own' sounds like 'fiendishly difficult'; literally it is the job the devil does, and the Tempter is one of his names.
explanation.definitionFit: Satan is called the Tempter because his work is luring people into sin.

clue.text: The best part of the dinner is this description of the man who needs it.

explanation.walkthrough: 'The inner man' is an old phrase for a person's stomach or appetite, which is what needs dinner.

clue.text: Part and parcel of every foot as we see when the shoe pinches.

definitions.text: Part and parcel of every foot

clue.text: A light in the sky

blocks.note: surface reading: a lamp or a single shining point
setter's reading: a hazy glowing patch among the stars

clue.text: As to the shoppers' burden, you can wager about the demand.

clue.text: Has driven many a good-man to drink.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Driven to drink' suggests despair; the setter means only the natural urge for liquid.

clue.text: Hardly as long as necessary but serves a similar purpose.

explanation.definitionFit: Need, as in 'there is no need', expresses what is required, much as necessary does.

clue.text: Conditions.

blocks.note: surface reading: circumstances or states, such as weather conditions
setter's reading: the stipulations of an agreement

explanation.walkthrough: A one-word clue: the answer is the word for the stipulations of a contract.

clue.text: A perfectly good stroke, and a pity to cut it just to make a display.

clue.text: What /we require here is an all round remedy.

clue.text: A firm order for a car.

clue.text: Deals with the transport of coal in the pits.

clue.text: This doesn't make summer,

blocks.note: surface reading: something fails to produce or cause

clue.text: Postman's knock.
